standard.title: Data Collection Techniques
standard.description: investigate techniques for data collection including census, sampling, experiment and observation, and explain the practicalities and implications of obtaining data through these techniques
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations and identify variable types (from AC9M7ST03, AC9M7ST01). Students understand sampling informally.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students distinguish census from sampling, identify appropriate collection techniques for different situations, and explain the practicalities, limitations and bias implications of each.

nodes.label: Census vs sampling and collection technique selection
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students distinguish census from sampling and identify when each is appropriate; describe the main data collection techniques.
nodes.minimum_width: State the difference between census and sampling; identify which is appropriate for a given situation and explain why.
nodes.typical_width: Compare census, sampling, experiment and observation as data collection techniques; evaluate each for practicality, cost, and appropriateness in varied contexts.
wider: Investigate how decisions concerning sampling relate to training AI systems — explain why biased sampling in training data leads to biased AI outputs.
Explore how digital measuring devices and simulations change the practicalities of data collection compared to manual methods.

response_modes.reason: Judgment about appropriate data collection technique requires encountering a wide range of contexts — scientific experiments, surveys, social studies, AI training. Students who only consider surveys miss the full range.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate collection techniques for appropriateness cannot identify sources of bias in Node 2 — the bias evaluation depends on first understanding what the technique does and who it includes or excludes.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: AI training data bias is a rich and contemporary extension — the connection between sampling decisions in statistics and the fairness of AI systems is genuinely significant and within Year 8 reach.
success_criteria: Identifies an appropriate collection technique for a given context and justifies the choice.
Explains at least one practical limitation of sampling.

nodes.label: Bias in data collection
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students recognise and explain sources of bias in data collection and describe how bias affects conclusions.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a source of bias in a described data collection process and explain its likely effect.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate data collection designs for potential bias; distinguish sampling bias, response bias, and measurement bias; suggest how to reduce bias.
wider: Investigate a real case of biased data collection and its consequences — connect to ethical implications of data misuse.
Explore how voluntary response bias occurs in online surveys and polls — investigate with a class experiment.

response_modes.reason: Identifying bias requires a systematic approach: who is included, who is excluded, how is the data collected, what might influence responses? Students who proceed intuitively miss systematic biases.

nodes.hinge_reason: Bias identification and evaluation is prerequisite for the entire AC9M8ST02–ST04 investigation chain — students who cannot recognise sources of bias produce unreliable sampling designs, analyses, and inferences in all subsequent statistics standards.
success_criteria: Identifies a source of bias in a data collection scenario.
Explains the likely direction and effect of the bias.
Suggests a concrete method to reduce the identified bias.
